expectedText:
UIFSA — REGISTRATION OF AN OUT-OF-STATE SUPPORT ORDER INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

DECLARATION IDENTIFYING THE ORDER AND AMOUNTS OWED
This registration concerns a support order issued in Texas, by District Court of Travis County, Texas, case/docket number D-1-FM-24-001234, dated March 1, 2022 (including any later modification of that order). The obligor (paying party) under the order is Taylor Morgan. The obligee (receiving party) under the order is Jordan Alex Lee. The order requires current support payments of $1,200 per month. Jordan Alex Lee, as the party requesting registration, states that as of September 1, 2026 the amount of arrears under the order is $3,600. This registration is being requested in San Francisco County County, California.

REGISTERING AN OUT-OF-STATE SUPPORT ORDER FOR ENFORCEMENT
California law allows a child- or spousal-support order issued by another state, or a foreign support order, to be registered in a California tribunal for enforcement. Registration is accomplished by sending specific records to the appropriate California tribunal: (1) a letter of transmittal requesting registration and enforcement; (2) two copies of the order to be registered, including any modification of the order, one of which must be a certified copy; (3) a sworn statement by the person requesting registration, or a certified statement by the custodian of the records, showing the amount of any arrearage; (4) the obligor's name and, if known, the obligor's address and Social Security number, the obligor's employer and other income sources, and a description and location of the obligor's property in California; and (5) the obligee's name and address (or, if applicable, the person to whom payments are to be remitted). If two or more orders are in effect for the same obligor and obligee, additional filings are required identifying every order asserted to be in effect and specifying which order is claimed to control.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A support order or income-withholding order issued in another state or a foreign support order may be registered in this state for enforcement."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 5700.601 (California Legislative Information text), authorization to register an out-of-state or foreign support order in California for enforcement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=5700.601.)
  "(a) Except as otherwise provided in Section 5700.706, a support order or income-withholding order of another state or a foreign support order may be registered in this state by sending the following records to the appropriate tribunal in this state: (1) a letter of transmittal to the tribunal requesting registration and enforcement; (2) two copies, including one certified copy, of the order to be registered, including any modification of the order; (3) a sworn statement by the person requesting registration or a certified statement by the custodian of the records showing the amount of any arrearage; (4) the name of the obligor and, if known: (A) the obligor’s address and social security number; (B) the name and address of the obligor’s employer and any other source of income of the obligor; and (C) a description and the location of property of the obligor in this state not exempt from execution; and (5) except as otherwise provided in Section 5700.312, the name and address of the obligee and, if applicable, the person to whom support payments are to be remitted."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 5700.602(a) (California Legislative Information text), the records that must be sent to the California tribunal to register an order for enforcement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=5700.602.)

Effective January 1, 2016, Stats. 2015, Ch. 493 (SB 646) repealed the former UIFSA part and recodified it, without substantive change to the numbering scheme used here, into Division 9, Part 6, at Family Code §§ 5700.101-5700.905. This was confirmed directly: a fetch of the old § 4900 on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov returns an empty code-text body (no text at that section number), while § 5700.101 et seq. contains the full current UIFSA text. All citations below use the current, correct §5700.xxx numbering. This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Fam. Code §§ 5700.601 and 5700.602(a), both within the same 2015 enactment (Stats. 2015, Ch. 493) that added this entire part, so they are not independent sources in the sense of separately-enacted law, only in the sense of being separately numbered provisions. This clause states the mechanics of registration only; it does not state whether a particular order is eligible for registration, does not itself accomplish registration, and does not address registration for modification (a meaningfully different process, covered in a separate clause in this document). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's enactment of the Uniform Interstate Family Support Act (UIFSA) actually works -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific support order. Every U.S. state, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories have enacted some version of UIFSA (the 2008 Act, as amended, per the federal mandate at 42 U.S.C. § 666(f)), but the codification location, section numbers, specific deadlines, and some procedural details differ state to state; this document describes California's specific enactment only. This document is informational only: it does not itself register, enforce, confirm, contest, or modify any support order, and does not determine whether a specific order or party qualifies for any of these procedures. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed almost entirely by statutory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session, given the statutory nature of the topic and CourtListener's limited daily quota.

CONTINUING, EXCLUSIVE JURISDICTION: ONLY ONE ORDER CONTROLS
UIFSA's central organizing principle is that, at any given time, only one state's child-support order controls, and the state that issued the controlling order generally keeps sole ('continuing, exclusive') jurisdiction to modify it. For a child-support order, a California tribunal that issued the order and whose order is the controlling order retains this jurisdiction only if, at the time a modification request is filed, California remains the residence of the obligor, the individual obligee, or the child, or the parties otherwise consent (in a record or in open court) to California continuing to exercise jurisdiction. If none of those conditions holds -- most notably, if none of the obligor, the obligee, or the child still lives in California -- California's basis for continuing, exclusive jurisdiction to modify its own child-support order no longer exists, and (as addressed in a separate clause) another state where a party resides may then be able to take up modification. Spousal-support orders work differently: the issuing state's continuing, exclusive jurisdiction to modify a spousal-support order it issued lasts for the entire existence of the support obligation, with no equivalent residency condition -- a real, non-obvious distinction from the child-support rule.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A tribunal of this state that has issued a child-support order consistent with the law of this state has and shall exercise continuing, exclusive jurisdiction to modify its child-support order if the order is the controlling order and: (1) at the time of the filing of a request for modification this state is the residence of the obligor, the individual obligee, or the child for whose benefit the support order is issued; or (2) even if this state is not the residence of the obligor, the individual obligee, or the child for whose benefit the support order is issued, the parties consent in a record or in open court that the tribunal of this state may continue to exercise jurisdiction to modify its order."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 5700.205(a) (California Legislative Information text), the conditions under which California retains continuing, exclusive jurisdiction to modify a child-support order it issued (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=5700.205.)
  "(a) A tribunal of this state issuing a spousal-support order consistent with the law of this state has continuing, exclusive jurisdiction to modify the spousal-support order throughout the existence of the support obligation."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 5700.211(a) (California Legislative Information text), continuing, exclusive jurisdiction over a spousal-support order lasting for the life of the obligation, without a residency condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=5700.211.)

REGISTRATION FOR MODIFICATION IS NOT THE SAME AS REGISTRATION FOR ENFORCEMENT
UIFSA treats registering an out-of-state child-support order to enforce it (collect ongoing payments or existing arrears under the order as written) differently from registering it to seek a modification of its terms. A party or support enforcement agency seeking to modify, or to modify and enforce, another state's child-support order must first register that order using the same enforcement-registration procedure described above; a petition for modification may then be filed with, or after, that registration, and the petition must state the grounds for modification. Registering the order, by itself, does not give a California tribunal the power to change its terms: California may modify a registered child-support order issued by another state only if, after notice and hearing, additional jurisdictional prerequisites are met -- either (1) none of the child, the individual obligee, or the obligor still resides in the issuing state, the party petitioning for modification is not a California resident, and the other party is subject to California's personal jurisdiction; or (2) California is the child's residence, or a party is subject to California's personal jurisdiction, and all individual parties have filed a record consenting to have California modify the order and assume continuing, exclusive jurisdiction over it. Absent one of those two pathways, a California tribunal that has registered another state's child-support order may enforce it but may not modify it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A party or support enforcement agency seeking to modify, or to modify and enforce, a child-support order issued in another state shall register that order in this state in the same manner provided in Sections 5700.601 through 5700.608 if the order has not been registered. A petition for modification may be filed at the same time as a request for registration, or later. The pleading must specify the grounds for modification."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 5700.609 (California Legislative Information text), the requirement to register a child-support order under the enforcement-registration procedure before seeking modification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=5700.609.)
  "(a) If Section 5700.613 does not apply, upon petition a tribunal of this state may modify a child-support order issued in another state which is registered in this state if, after notice and hearing, the tribunal finds that: (1) the following requirements are met: (A) neither the child, nor the obligee who is an individual, nor the obligor resides in the issuing state; (B) a petitioner who is a nonresident of this state seeks modification; and (C) the respondent is subject to the personal jurisdiction of the tribunal of this state; or (2) this state is the residence of the child, or a party who is an individual is subject to the personal jurisdiction of the tribunal of this state, and all of the parties who are individuals have filed consents in a record in the issuing tribunal for a tribunal of this state to modify the support order and assume continuing, exclusive jurisdiction."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 5700.611(a) (California Legislative Information text), the additional jurisdictional prerequisites California requires before it may modify a registered child-support order issued by another state (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=5700.611.)

CONTESTING A REGISTERED SUPPORT ORDER: LIMITED, ENUMERATED DEFENSES
A party who did not register the order (the nonregistering party) may contest its validity or enforcement, but only by requesting a hearing within a deadline set by a separate statute, and only on specific, enumerated grounds -- the contest right is not open-ended. If the nonregistering party does not timely request a hearing, the order is confirmed by operation of law without any further proceeding. A party who does request a hearing has the burden of proving one or more of eight listed defenses: (1) the issuing tribunal lacked personal jurisdiction over the contesting party; (2) the order was obtained by fraud; (3) the order has been vacated, suspended, or modified by a later order; (4) the issuing tribunal has stayed the order pending appeal; (5) there is a defense under California law to the specific remedy being sought; (6) full or partial payment has already been made; (7) a statute of limitations bars enforcement of some or all of the alleged arrears; or (8) the order asserted to be the controlling order is not actually the controlling order. This list is longer, and more specific, than a bare 'the order is wrong' objection -- a contest that does not fit one of these eight grounds does not defeat registration.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A nonregistering party seeking to contest the validity or enforcement of a registered support order in this state shall request a hearing within the time required by Section 5700.605. The nonregistering party may seek to vacate the registration, to assert any defense to an allegation of noncompliance with the registered order, or to contest the remedies being sought or the amount of any alleged arrearages pursuant to Section 5700.607. (b) If the nonregistering party fails to contest the validity or enforcement of the registered support order in a timely manner, the order is confirmed by operation of law."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 5700.606(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the requirement to timely request a hearing to contest a registered order, and automatic confirmation by operation of law if none is requested (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=5700.606.)
  "(a) A party contesting the validity or enforcement of a registered support order or seeking to vacate the registration has the burden of proving one or more of the following defenses: (1) the issuing tribunal lacked personal jurisdiction over the contesting party; (2) the order was obtained by fraud; (3) the order has been vacated, suspended, or modified by a later order; (4) the issuing tribunal has stayed the order pending appeal; (5) there is a defense under the law of this state to the remedy sought; (6) full or partial payment has been made; (7) the statute of limitation under Section 5700.604 precludes enforcement of some or all of the alleged arrearages; or (8) the alleged controlling order is not the controlling order."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 5700.607(a) (California Legislative Information text), the enumerated list of defenses, and the contesting party's burden of proof (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=5700.607.)

EFFECT OF REGISTRATION AND CONFIRMATION
Once an out-of-state or foreign support order is registered in California, it becomes enforceable in the same manner, and subject to the same procedures, as an order that a California tribunal issued itself -- California courts recognize and enforce it, but (subject to the separate modification pathway addressed elsewhere in this document) may not modify it, as long as the issuing tribunal had jurisdiction when it issued the order. Confirmation of the registered order -- whether that happens automatically by operation of law because no timely contest was filed, or affirmatively after a contest hearing -- has a further, distinct effect: it forecloses raising, in any later proceeding, any matter that could have been raised as a defense at the time of registration. In other words, confirmation is not merely a formality; it operates as a final determination that cuts off previously-available objections.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(b) A registered support order issued in another state or a foreign country is enforceable in the same manner and is subject to the same procedures as an order issued by a tribunal of this state. (c) Except as otherwise provided in this part, a tribunal of this state shall recognize and enforce, but may not modify, a registered support order if the issuing tribunal had jurisdiction."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 5700.603(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information text), a registered order becomes enforceable as if issued by a California tribunal, but may not be modified if the issuing tribunal had jurisdiction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=5700.603.)
  "Confirmation of a registered support order, whether by operation of law or after notice and hearing, precludes further contest of the order with respect to any matter that could have been asserted at the time of registration."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 5700.608 (California Legislative Information text), confirmation of a registered order precludes further contest of matters that could have been raised at registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=5700.608.)

CHOICE OF LAW FOR ARREARS AND INTEREST VERSUS CALIFORNIA'S OWN ENFORCEMENT PROCEDURES
UIFSA splits which state's law applies to a registered support order along substance-versus-procedure lines. The substantive law of the issuing state (or foreign country) governs the nature, extent, amount, and duration of current payments; the computation of arrearages and the accrual of interest on those arrearages; and the existence and satisfaction of other obligations under the order. For the statute of limitations specifically, whichever period is longer -- California's or the issuing state's -- applies to an arrears proceeding, a pro-enforcement rule rather than a strict issuing-state-controls rule. At the same time, the California tribunal enforcing the order applies California's own procedures and remedies to enforce current support and collect arrears and interest -- the forum state's procedural law governs the mechanics of enforcement even though the issuing state's substantive law governs the amounts owed. Once a tribunal determines which of two or more competing orders controls and consolidates the arrears, a California tribunal must then prospectively apply the controlling order's state's law -- including its interest-on-arrears rules -- going forward for current, future, and consolidated support.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]

(b) In a proceeding for arrears under a registered support order, the statute of limitation of this state, or of the issuing state or foreign country, whichever is longer, applies."
  — Cal. Fam.   "(c) A responding tribunal of this state shall apply the procedures and remedies of this state to enforce current support and collect arrears and interest due on a support order of another state or a foreign country registered in this state.   — Cal. Fam. California law allows a child- or spousal-support order issued by another state, or a foreign support order, to be registered in a California tribunal for enforcement. If two or more orders are in effect for the same obligor and obligee, additional filings are required identifying every order asserted to be in effect and specifying which order is claimed to control.

expectedJSON.body: UIFSA's central organizing principle is that, at any given time, only one state's child-support order controls, and the state that issued the controlling order generally keeps sole ('continuing, exclusive') jurisdiction to modify it. For a child-support order, a California tribunal that issued the order and whose order is the controlling order retains this jurisdiction only if, at the time a modification request is filed, California remains the residence of the obligor, the individual obligee, or the child, or the parties otherwise consent (in a record or in open court) to California continuing to exercise jurisdiction. If none of those conditions holds -- most notably, if none of the obligor, the obligee, or the child still lives in California -- California's basis for continuing, exclusive jurisdiction to modify its own child-support order no longer exists, and (as addressed in a separate clause) another state where a party resides may then be able to take up modification. Spousal-support orders work differently: the issuing state's continuing, exclusive jurisdiction to modify a spousal-support order it issued lasts for the entire existence of the support obligation, with no equivalent residency condition -- a real, non-obvious distinction from the child-support rule.

citations.quote: (a) A tribunal of this state that has issued a child-support order consistent with the law of this state has and shall exercise continuing, exclusive jurisdiction to modify its child-support order if the order is the controlling order and: (1) at the time of the filing of a request for modification this state is the residence of the obligor, the individual obligee, or the child for whose benefit the support order is issued; or (2) even if this state is not the residence of the obligor, the individual obligee, or the child for whose benefit the support order is issued, the parties consent in a record or in open court that the tribunal of this state may continue to exercise jurisdiction to modify its order.

citations.quote: (a) A tribunal of this state issuing a spousal-support order consistent with the law of this state has continuing, exclusive jurisdiction to modify the spousal-support order throughout the existence of the support obligation.

expectedJSON.body: UIFSA treats registering an out-of-state child-support order to enforce it (collect ongoing payments or existing arrears under the order as written) differently from registering it to seek a modification of its terms. A party or support enforcement agency seeking to modify, or to modify and enforce, another state's child-support order must first register that order using the same enforcement-registration procedure described above; a petition for modification may then be filed with, or after, that registration, and the petition must state the grounds for modification. Registering the order, by itself, does not give a California tribunal the power to change its terms: California may modify a registered child-support order issued by another state only if, after notice and hearing, additional jurisdictional prerequisites are met -- either (1) none of the child, the individual obligee, or the obligor still resides in the issuing state, the party petitioning for modification is not a California resident, and the other party is subject to California's personal jurisdiction; or (2) California is the child's residence, or a party is subject to California's personal jurisdiction, and all individual parties have filed a record consenting to have California modify the order and assume continuing, exclusive jurisdiction over it. Absent one of those two pathways, a California tribunal that has registered another state's child-support order may enforce it but may not modify it.

A petition for modification may be filed at the same time as a request for registration, or later. The pleading must specify the grounds for modification.

expectedJSON.body: A party who did not register the order (the nonregistering party) may contest its validity or enforcement, but only by requesting a hearing within a deadline set by a separate statute, and only on specific, enumerated grounds -- the contest right is not open-ended. If the nonregistering party does not timely request a hearing, the order is confirmed by operation of law without any further proceeding. A party who does request a hearing has the burden of proving one or more of eight listed defenses: (1) the issuing tribunal lacked personal jurisdiction over the contesting party; (2) the order was obtained by fraud; (3) the order has been vacated, suspended, or modified by a later order; (4) the issuing tribunal has stayed the order pending appeal; (5) there is a defense under California law to the specific remedy being sought; (6) full or partial payment has already been made; (7) a statute of limitations bars enforcement of some or all of the alleged arrears; or (8) the order asserted to be the controlling order is not actually the controlling order. This list is longer, and more specific, than a bare 'the order is wrong' objection -- a contest that does not fit one of these eight grounds does not defeat registration.

citations.quote: (a) A nonregistering party seeking to contest the validity or enforcement of a registered support order in this state shall request a hearing within the time required by Section 5700.605. The nonregistering party may seek to vacate the registration, to assert any defense to an allegation of noncompliance with the registered order, or to contest the remedies being sought or the amount of any alleged arrearages pursuant to Section 5700.607. (b) If the nonregistering party fails to contest the validity or enforcement of the registered support order in a timely manner, the order is confirmed by operation of law.

expectedJSON.body: Once an out-of-state or foreign support order is registered in California, it becomes enforceable in the same manner, and subject to the same procedures, as an order that a California tribunal issued itself -- California courts recognize and enforce it, but (subject to the separate modification pathway addressed elsewhere in this document) may not modify it, as long as the issuing tribunal had jurisdiction when it issued the order. Confirmation of the registered order -- whether that happens automatically by operation of law because no timely contest was filed, or affirmatively after a contest hearing -- has a further, distinct effect: it forecloses raising, in any later proceeding, any matter that could have been raised as a defense at the time of registration. In other words, confirmation is not merely a formality; it operates as a final determination that cuts off previously-available objections.

(c) Except as otherwise provided in this part, a tribunal of this state shall recognize and enforce, but may not modify, a registered support order if the issuing tribunal had jurisdiction.

expectedJSON.body: UIFSA splits which state's law applies to a registered support order along substance-versus-procedure lines. The substantive law of the issuing state (or foreign country) governs the nature, extent, amount, and duration of current payments; the computation of arrearages and the accrual of interest on those arrearages; and the existence and satisfaction of other obligations under the order. For the statute of limitations specifically, whichever period is longer -- California's or the issuing state's -- applies to an arrears proceeding, a pro-enforcement rule rather than a strict issuing-state-controls rule. At the same time, the California tribunal enforcing the order applies California's own procedures and remedies to enforce current support and collect arrears and interest -- the forum state's procedural law governs the mechanics of enforcement even though the issuing state's substantive law governs the amounts owed. Once a tribunal determines which of two or more competing orders controls and consolidates the arrears, a California tribunal must then prospectively apply the controlling order's state's law -- including its interest-on-arrears rules -- going forward for current, future, and consolidated support.

citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise provided in subsection (d), the law of the issuing state or foreign country governs: (1) the nature, extent, amount, and duration of current payments under a registered support order; (2) the computation and payment of arrearages and accrual of interest on the arrearages under the support order; and (3) the existence and satisfaction of other obligations under the support order. (b) In a proceeding for arrears under a registered support order, the statute of limitation of this state, or of the issuing state or foreign country, whichever is longer, applies.

citations.cite: California's own procedures govern the mechanics of enforcement, and the controlling order's state's law applies prospectively once determined
citations.quote: (c) A responding tribunal of this state shall apply the procedures and remedies of this state to enforce current support and collect arrears and interest due on a support order of another state or a foreign country registered in this state. (d) After a tribunal of this state or another state determines which is the controlling order and issues an order consolidating arrears, if any, a tribunal of this state shall prospectively apply the law of the state or foreign country issuing the controlling order, including its law on interest on arrears, on current and future support, and on consolidated arrears.
